question: Which Portuguese navigator, in 1498, became the first European to reach India by sailing around the southern tip of Africa?
topic: Famous explorers and voyages of discovery
source_excerpt: Da Gama finally accomplished the feat when he landed at Kozhikode on 20 May 1498.

extra.why_interesting: Players know Columbus sailed west looking for India; the man who actually got there by sea, going the other way round Africa, is the one who changed world trade.
extra.verification_notes: Vasco da Gama reached Calicut on 20 May 1498 as the first European to arrive by the sea route around Africa; the question's wording excludes the earlier overland travellers.

explanation: Da Gama landed at Calicut on India's southwest coast, giving Portugal the sea route to Asian spices that Columbus had failed to find by going west.

question: On which Pacific islands was the British navigator James Cook killed in 1779, during his third great voyage?
topic: Famous explorers and voyages of discovery
source_excerpt: Cook and four marines were killed in the affray and left on the shore.

extra.why_interesting: The man who charted New Zealand and Australia's east coast did not die at sea or at home, but in a beach skirmish on a holiday island everyone can name.
extra.verification_notes: Cook was killed 14 Feb 1779 at Kealakekua Bay, Hawaiʻi Island, in the Hawaiian Islands, on his third voyage (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Cook).

explanation: Cook died in a fight with islanders at Kealakekua Bay on the Big Island of Hawaii, after a dispute over a stolen boat turned violent.

question: In May 1953, New Zealander Edmund Hillary and Sherpa Tenzing Norgay became the first people confirmed to stand on the top of which mountain?
topic: Famous explorers and voyages of discovery
source_excerpt: On 29 May 1953, he and Edmund Hillary were the first people confirmed to have reached the summit of Mount Everest

extra.why_interesting: A great twentieth-century exploration first that most adults have heard of; the delight is remembering it was a two-man partnership, not a solo hero.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Hillary and Tenzing were the first confirmed to summit Mount Everest on 29 May 1953; the question's 'confirmed' wording handles the Mallory and Irvine 1924 uncertainty.

explanation: Hillary and Tenzing reached the 8,849-metre summit on the 29th of May 1953, and the news reached London just in time for Queen Elizabeth's coronation.

question: Marco Polo's famous book about his travels to the court of Kublai Khan was dictated to a fellow inmate while Polo was being held where?
topic: Famous explorers and voyages of discovery
source_excerpt: He spent several months of his imprisonment dictating a detailed account of his travels to a fellow inmate, Rustichello da Pisa.

extra.why_interesting: Players picture the famous travel book written at a Venetian desk; in fact it was told from a prison cell to a cellmate, after Polo was captured in a sea battle.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Polo dictated the account to fellow inmate Rustichello da Pisa while imprisoned by the Genoese; the answer 'in prison' is generic but correct.

explanation: Polo was captured by Genoa after a sea battle with Venice, and in a Genoese prison he told his stories to the romance writer Rustichello da Pisa, who wrote them down.

question: When Bartolomeu Dias first rounded the southern tip of Africa in 1488, he gave it a gloomier name than the one it carries today. What did he call it?
topic: Famous explorers and voyages of discovery
source_excerpt: Tradition has it that Dias originally named it the Cape of Storms (Cabo das Tormentas) and that King John II later renamed it the Cape of Good Hope

extra.why_interesting: The cheerful name on every map today was a royal rebranding; the man who actually sailed round it chose something far more honest.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's Bartolomeu Dias article says he originally named it Cape of Storms (Cabo das Tormentas) and John II renamed it Cape of Good Hope; the 'tradition' hedge and the loose 'southern tip' wording are minor.

explanation: Dias named it after the foul weather that nearly wrecked him, but King John II of Portugal renamed it the Cape of Good Hope to advertise the promise of a sea route to India.

question: Years before he reached the South Pole, Roald Amundsen became the first person to sail all the way through which long-sought Arctic sea route north of Canada?
topic: Famous explorers and voyages of discovery
source_excerpt: In 1903, Amundsen led the first expedition to traverse Canada's Northwest Passage between the Atlantic and Pacific oceans.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone files Amundsen under the South Pole; few realise he had already solved the centuries-old Arctic puzzle that had killed Franklin's expedition.
extra.verification_notes: Amundsen's Gjøa expedition (1903–1906) was the first to traverse the Northwest Passage, years before reaching the South Pole in 1911.

explanation: Amundsen took the tiny ship Gjøa through the passage between 1903 and 1906, succeeding where John Franklin's expedition had vanished sixty years earlier.

question: Three of these navigators personally sailed all the way around the world. Which one never did?
topic: Famous explorers and voyages of discovery
source_excerpt: Magellan died on April 27, 1521, in the Philippines during the Battle of Mactan

extra.why_interesting: The name most associated with the first voyage around the world belongs to the one man on the list who never finished one.
extra.verification_notes: Magellan died at Mactan in 1521; Elcano, Drake and Cavendish each completed a circumnavigation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Magellan).

explanation: Magellan was killed on the island of Mactan in the Philippines in 1521, halfway round. Elcano brought his expedition home, and Drake and Cavendish later completed their own circumnavigations.

question: The only confirmed Viking settlement in North America, dating from around the year 1000, was excavated at L'Anse aux Meadows. In which modern country is it?
topic: Famous explorers and voyages of discovery
source_excerpt: L'Anse aux Meadows is the only confirmed Norse site in North America outside Greenland.

extra.why_interesting: Players know the Vikings 'got to America first' but rarely know the one place where archaeology actually proves it, and that it is Canadian, not American.
extra.verification_notes: L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, Canada, is still the only confirmed Norse site in North America outside Greenland, and no newer confirmed site has been found (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%27Anse_aux_Meadows).

explanation: The site sits at the northern tip of Newfoundland and is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site, the physical proof that Norse sailors reached the Americas five centuries before Columbus.

question: Which English explorer was cast adrift in a small boat by his mutinous crew in 1611, in the great Canadian bay that now carries his name?
topic: Famous explorers and voyages of discovery
source_excerpt: set Hudson, his teenage son John, and seven crewmen—men who were either sick and infirm or loyal to Hudson—adrift from Discovery in a small shallop

extra.why_interesting: A huge sea on the world map carries the name of a man whose own crew abandoned him there to die; the geography is the clue to the name.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Hudson was set adrift in a shallop by mutineers in 1611 in Hudson Bay, which is named after him.

explanation: Hudson, his teenage son and seven others were set adrift and never seen again, while the mutineers sailed the ship home to England.

question: Roughly 270 men sailed from Spain with Magellan's fleet in 1519. About how many of them came home on the single ship that completed the voyage around the world in 1522?
topic: Famous explorers and voyages of discovery
source_excerpt: 18 men returned to Seville aboard Victoria in 1522

extra.why_interesting: Players expect heavy losses on a three-year voyage, but the sheer scale, with fewer than one in ten coming home, is still a shock.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia reports about 270 men departing and only 18 returning aboard Victoria (about 21 with three Moluccans), both under 25.

explanation: Just 18 survivors reached Spain aboard the Victoria under Juan Sebastián Elcano, after scurvy, battles, desertions and a shipwreck had claimed the rest and four of the five ships.

question: Decades before Portuguese ships reached the Indian Ocean, which Chinese admiral led seven huge fleet voyages that sailed as far as the east coast of Africa?
topic: Famous explorers and voyages of discovery
source_excerpt: commanded seven treasure voyages across Asia

extra.why_interesting: Players assume long-range exploration began with Portugal and Spain; a Chinese fleet was visiting East Africa decades before Dias rounded the Cape.
extra.verification_notes: Zheng He commanded seven treasure voyages (1405–1433) reaching East Africa, decades before da Gama's 1498 arrival, per Wikipedia.

explanation: Between 1405 and 1433 Zheng He's treasure fleets visited India, Arabia and East African ports such as Malindi, and one voyage famously brought a giraffe back to the Ming emperor.

question: Which 14th-century scholar from Tangier spent nearly thirty years travelling around 120,000 kilometres across Africa, the Middle East, India and China, out-distancing Marco Polo?
topic: Famous explorers and voyages of discovery
source_excerpt: totalling around 117,000 km (73,000 mi), surpassing Zheng He with about 50,000 km (31,000 mi) and Marco Polo with 24,000 km (15,000 mi).

extra.why_interesting: Marco Polo gets the fame, but a Moroccan contemporary out-travelled him by a wide margin, and his name is a genuine reach for a well-read player.
extra.verification_notes: Ibn Battuta, a scholar from Tangier, travelled about 30 years and roughly 117,000 km (about 120,000 km), well beyond Marco Polo's 24,000 km.

explanation: Ibn Battuta set out for Mecca in 1325 and kept going for almost three decades, and his dictated account, the Rihla, remains a key record of the medieval Islamic world.

question: Magellan set out from Spain in 1519 with a fleet of five ships. How many of those ships made it all the way around the world and back to Spain in 1522?
topic: Famous explorers and voyages of discovery

extra.why_interesting: Players picture the 'first voyage around the world' as a triumphant fleet coming home; in fact the expedition was nearly wiped out, with a single battered ship and a skeleton crew limping back, and Magellan himself not among them.

explanation: Only the Victoria returned, carrying just 18 of the roughly 270 men who had set out, and Magellan himself had been killed in the Philippines a year earlier.

question: Antonio Pigafetta kept a careful day-by-day diary on Magellan's expedition. When the last surviving ship reached Spain in 1522 after sailing west around the globe, by how much was his diary out of step with the calendar at home?
topic: Famous explorers and voyages of discovery
source_excerpt: We were greatly surprised for it was Wednesday with us, and we could not see how we had made a mistake

extra.why_interesting: Players assume a meticulous diary cannot drift from the calendar. The answer makes them realise that sailing around the world westward quietly costs you a full day, a problem nobody had met before because nobody had done it before, and the international date line did not yet exist to fix it.
extra.verification_notes: Pigafetta's diary said Wednesday when the Portuguese at Cape Verde said Thursday (9 July 1522), a one-day lag from circumnavigating westward; source https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_First_Voyage_Round_the_World/Pigafetta's_Account_of_Magellan's_Voyage

explanation: Sailing steadily westward, the crew had lost a full day without noticing, and no international date line yet existed to account for it. Pigafetta thought he had made a counting error until the explanation was worked out.

question: The dodo, the most famous extinct bird of all, lived on just one Indian Ocean island. Which one?
source_excerpt: The dodo (Raphus cucullatus) is an extinct flightless bird that was endemic to Mauritius, an island east of Madagascar in the Indian Ocean.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone knows the dodo is dead; far fewer can place its home, yet 'Indian Ocean island' narrows it to a short, guessable list.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the dodo was endemic to Mauritius, and no newer development contradicts this.

explanation: Dutch sailors reached Mauritius in 1598, and within about ninety years the trusting, flightless dodo was gone.

question: Among emperor penguins, which parent spends the Antarctic winter balancing the single egg on its feet, going around two months without food?
source_excerpt: By the time the egg hatches, the male will have fasted for around 120 days since arriving at the colony.

extra.why_interesting: The default assumption is that the mother sits on the egg; in the harshest nursery on Earth it is the father who starves in the dark.
extra.verification_notes: Male emperor penguins incubate the egg on their feet through the winter. The 'two months' figure is loose, since the total fast is about 120 days, but it doesn't affect the answer. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_penguin

explanation: The female lays the egg and heads to sea to feed, while the male huddles with thousands of other dads at minus forty, losing up to half his body weight.

question: In Greek myth, Icarus fell to his death when he flew too close to the sun. What part of his wings melted?
source_excerpt: the heat from the Sun softened and melted the wax. Icarus could feel melted wax dripping down his arms.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone remembers that Icarus flew too close to the sun; the question checks whether they remember what actually failed.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's Icarus article states the wings' feathers were held on by beeswax, which the sun's heat melted.

explanation: His father Daedalus built the wings from feathers bound with wax, and warned him to fly neither too low near the sea nor too high near the sun.

question: Which small seabird enjoys two summers every year by commuting between the top and the bottom of the world, the longest migration of any animal?
source_excerpt: by far the longest migrations known in the animal kingdom

extra.why_interesting: The 'two summers a year' hook sounds like a riddle, and the answer is a small, unglamorous seabird rather than a mighty albatross or eagle.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the Arctic tern has the longest known animal migration, and no newer record-holder was found.

explanation: Tracked terns cover around seventy thousand kilometres a year, so over a long life one bird can fly the equivalent of three trips to the Moon and back.

question: In 1783 the Montgolfier brothers sent the first living passengers up in a hot-air balloon at Versailles: a sheep, a rooster, and which water bird?
source_excerpt: a sheep called Montauciel ("Climb-to-the-sky"), a duck and a rooster

extra.why_interesting: Players picture a brave aristocrat as the first balloon passenger; it was a barnyard trio, and the water bird is deducible once you know it had to be a common French farm animal.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the 1783 Versailles flight carried a sheep, a duck and a rooster.

explanation: The duck was the control subject, since it could already fly and would show whether any harm came from the balloon itself rather than the altitude.

question: In 2009 a pilot nicknamed Sully landed an airliner on the Hudson River after both engines failed. Which birds had been sucked into them?
source_excerpt: The bird remains were later identified by DNA testing to be Canada geese, which typically weigh more than engines are designed to withstand ingesting.

extra.why_interesting: The 'Miracle on the Hudson' is famous for the pilot; fewer people remember the culprits, though 'large birds near New York' points firmly in one direction.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's article on US Airways Flight 1549 says DNA testing identified the ingested birds as Canada geese; the pilot and date also match.

explanation: The Airbus hit a flock of Canada geese barely two minutes after take-off from LaGuardia, and all 155 people on board survived the water landing.

question: Each autumn, bar-tailed godwits leave Alaska and fly non-stop across the Pacific for over a week. Which island nation is the famous end of the journey?
source_excerpt: an eight-day non-stop flight from western Alaska to the Piako River near Thames

extra.why_interesting: A week in the air without food, water or sleep sounds impossible; the destination is reasoned out by thinking 'where is far south across the Pacific'.
extra.verification_notes: Bar-tailed godwits (baueri) fly non-stop from Alaska to New Zealand in about 8+ days; Australia is a minor alternative but not an 'island nation' answer.

explanation: That is roughly eleven thousand kilometres without landing, eating or drinking, and the birds burn so much fat that their digestive organs shrink before departure.

question: A giraffe, like you, has just seven bones in its neck. Roughly how many neck bones does a swan have?

possible_answers.a: Seven, the same as a giraffe

source_excerpt: Swans have 24 or more neck vertebrae; the mute swan (Cygnus olor) displays 23 vertebrae in the neck in one research study.

extra.why_interesting: The giraffe's absurd neck sets up the expectation of dozens of bones; the stem reveals it has seven, and the player must decide whether a swan's flexible neck beats that.
extra.verification_notes: Swans have roughly 22-25 cervical vertebrae (e.g., mute swan ~23-25), so 'More than twenty' is correct; the question's other claims hold (giraffe and humans have 7), and the count cannot go stale. Only search summaries were available, not the pages.

explanation: Mammals are locked at seven whatever their neck length, but birds are free to add vertebrae, and a swan carries more than twenty, which is why it can curl its neck into an S.

question: The highest bird flight ever confirmed ended when an African vulture struck an airliner at over 11 kilometres up in 1973. Which species of vulture was it?
source_excerpt: A Rüppell's vulture was confirmed to have passed into an aircraft engine of an airplane flying over Abidjan, Ivory Coast on 29 November 1973 at an altitude of 11,300 m

extra.why_interesting: Players assume high flyers are eagles or geese over the Himalayas; the record belongs to an African scavenger that reached cruising altitude of a jet.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms a Rüppell's vulture struck an aircraft at 11,300 m over Abidjan on 29 Nov 1973, still the highest confirmed bird altitude.

explanation: At that altitude the air holds about a quarter of the oxygen at sea level, and the vulture's blood is specially tuned to grab what little there is.

question: Three of these New Zealand birds have lost the power of flight. Which one still flies?
source_excerpt: it is one of the few parrot species in the world to regularly spend time above the tree line.

extra.why_interesting: All four are iconic New Zealand birds with similar-sounding Māori names, so nothing on the surface separates them; the player has to know which one never gave up the air.
extra.verification_notes: Kakapo, kiwi and takahē are flightless while the kea is a flying alpine parrot, so Kea is the only one that flies (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kea).

explanation: The kea is a mountain parrot famous for dismantling car wipers and backpacks, and it flies perfectly well, unlike the kakapo, the kiwi and the takahē.

question: Which global news agency, founded by a German-born entrepreneur, got its start in 1850 by flying stock prices between Aachen and Brussels with carrier pigeons?
source_excerpt: developed a prototype news service in Aachen using homing pigeons and electric telegraphy ... to transmit messages between Brussels and Aachen.

extra.why_interesting: A global news giant associated with screens and wires started with birds in a basket; 'Aachen to Brussels' plus 'German-born founder' gives a thinking player a real route to the name.
extra.verification_notes: Reuters was founded by German-born Paul Julius Reuter, who used pigeons between Aachen and Brussels; sources vary slightly between 1850 and 1851 for the pigeon service, but the answer is unambiguous.

explanation: Paul Reuter's pigeons beat the train by hours across the gap in the telegraph line, and he moved to London the next year to found the agency that still bears his name.

question: Scientists fitted tiny data loggers to common swifts and discovered they can stay in the air without landing once. Roughly how long can a swift remain continuously airborne?
source_excerpt: Swifts are airborne for more than 99% of the time during their 10-month non-breeding period; some individuals never settled.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume every bird must land to sleep, so they reach for 'days' or 'weeks'; the real answer is almost an entire year without touching anything.
extra.verification_notes: Hedenström et al. 2016 (Current Biology) showed common swifts remain airborne ~10 months without landing, so 'Months' is correct; no newer finding contradicts it.

explanation: Tracked swifts stayed aloft for around ten months straight, outside the breeding season, apparently sleeping in short bursts while gliding at altitude.

question: Which birds are the only ones able to fly backwards under their own power?
source_excerpt: In the class Aves (birds), there is only one family, Trochilidae (hummingbirds) where the backward flying phenomenon can be found.

extra.why_interesting: Players picture flight as strictly forward motion; realising one family of birds can calmly reverse out of a flower is a small delight, and the answer clicks once they think of the tiniest birds.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's Backward flying article says hummingbirds are the only bird family capable of backward flight; popular claims of brief backward movement in other birds are anecdotal.

explanation: A hummingbird's wing rotates almost fully at the shoulder, so both the forward and return stroke produce lift, letting it hover, reverse and even fly briefly upside down.

question: A sealed jar of honey left in a cupboard for twenty years is still safe to eat, while jam or syrup would have gone mouldy long ago. Why doesn't honey spoil?
correct_answer: Too little free water for microbes
alternative_answers: Sugar draws water out of bacteria
Too much sugar for bacteria to grow
It is acidic and has almost no water
headline_answer: Too little free water for microbes
topic: Chemistry of the kitchen and household
source_excerpt: So long as its water concentration does not rise much above 18%, honey has an indefinite shelf life, both within the hive and after its removal by a beekeeper.

extra.verification_notes: Honey's low water activity (high sugar, ~15-18% water) is the principal reason it resists spoilage, per Wikipedia's Honey article.

explanation: Spoilage is caused by bacteria and mould, and they need water to grow. Honey is about 80 percent sugar, and that sugar binds almost all of its water, so the small amount that remains is unavailable to any microbe. Honey is also mildly acidic, and the bees' enzymes produce a little hydrogen peroxide in it, which adds to the hostile environment. Any bacterium landing in honey has water pulled out of it by osmosis and dies. The only way honey spoils is if moisture gets in, which is why an open jar in a humid kitchen can eventually ferment.

question: Throwing a handful of baking soda on a small pan fire helps put it out because the heat makes it release which gas?
topic: Chemistry of the kitchen and household
source_excerpt: Sodium bicarbonate can be used to extinguish small grease or electrical fires by being thrown over the fire, as heating of sodium bicarbonate releases carbon dioxide.

extra.why_interesting: Players know not to throw water on a pan fire, but few realise the humble baking-soda tub is a mini extinguisher that works by chemistry, not by smothering with powder.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms that heating sodium bicarbonate releases carbon dioxide, which is why it can smother small grease fires; water vapor is also released but CO2 is the standard answer.

explanation: The hot powder breaks down and blankets the flames with carbon dioxide, starving them of oxygen. Never use water or flour, which can turn a grease fire into a fireball.

question: True or false: the natural gas piped to kitchen stoves has a strong rotten-egg smell of its own.
topic: Chemistry of the kitchen and household
source_excerpt: Because natural gas is odorless, a commercial odorizer, such as methanethiol, that smells of hydrogen sulfide (rotten eggs) is added to the gas for the ready detection of gas leaks.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone knows the 'gas smell', so the claim feels obviously true. The twist is that the smell is a deliberate additive, and the gas itself would kill you silently.
extra.verification_notes: Natural gas is odorless; the rotten-egg smell comes from an added odorant (mercaptans), so 'False' is correct per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_gas

explanation: Natural gas is almost pure methane and has no smell at all. Utilities add a tiny amount of a sulfur compound so that even a small leak is noticed immediately.

question: The chalky limescale that builds up inside kettles is mostly a carbonate of which element?
topic: Chemistry of the kitchen and household
source_excerpt: Limescale is a hard, chalky deposit consisting mainly of calcium carbonate (CaCO3).

extra.why_interesting: The 'lime' in limescale points nowhere obvious. Linking it to the same stuff as chalk and seashells makes the vinegar-descaling trick suddenly make sense.
extra.verification_notes: Kettle limescale is predominantly calcium carbonate (CaCO3), per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limescale; magnesium salts are only minor components.

explanation: It is essentially the same mineral as chalk and seashells, left behind when hard water is boiled. Vinegar dissolves it because the acid reacts with the carbonate, which is why descaling fizzes.

question: Ordinary household vinegar is roughly what percentage acetic acid, with the rest being mostly water?
topic: Chemistry of the kitchen and household
source_excerpt: Vinegar typically contains from 4% to 18% acetic acid by volume.

extra.why_interesting: Vinegar tastes so sharp that players guess it is mostly acid. The payoff is that it is overwhelmingly water, and the pure acid would be a corrosive hazard.
extra.verification_notes: Household table vinegar is about 4–8% acetic acid, so 'Around 5 percent' is the only fitting option; the Wikipedia page gives a 4–18% range overall, with the higher end being specialty vinegars.

explanation: Standard table vinegar is about five percent acetic acid. Pure acetic acid is a corrosive liquid that would burn your skin, so the water is doing most of the work in the bottle.

question: Fresh pineapple stops a gelatine jelly from setting, yet tinned pineapple works fine. What kind of substance in the fresh fruit is destroyed by the canning heat?
topic: Chemistry of the kitchen and household
source_excerpt: Cooked or canned pineapple does not have a tenderizing effect, as the enzymes are heat-labile and denatured in the cooking process.

extra.why_interesting: The fresh-versus-tinned contrast is the foothold: heat destroys something fragile. Players who reason 'heat kills what kind of thing?' land on enzyme and feel clever.
extra.verification_notes: Bromelain, a heat-labile protease enzyme in fresh pineapple, digests gelatin and is denatured by canning (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bromelain).

explanation: The enzyme bromelain chops up the gelatine proteins before they can form a gel. The same enzyme is why fresh pineapple makes your mouth feel tingly, since it is digesting you slightly too.

question: The yeast that makes bread dough rise produces carbon dioxide and which other substance, most of which is driven off in the oven?
topic: Chemistry of the kitchen and household
source_excerpt: Carbon dioxide and ethanol vapors produced during yeast fermentation result in bread's air pockets.

extra.why_interesting: Players know yeast makes beer and that yeast makes bread rise, but rarely connect the two. The idea that every loaf is briefly alcoholic is a delightful link.
extra.verification_notes: Yeast fermentation yields CO2 and ethanol, and most of the ethanol evaporates during baking; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bread.

explanation: It is the same fermentation that makes beer and wine, so raw risen dough contains a little ethanol. The heat of baking evaporates nearly all of it, which is part of that lovely bakery smell.

question: Egg dishes tarnish silver spoons unusually fast. The black tarnish is a compound of silver and which element, the same one behind the smell of rotten eggs?
topic: Chemistry of the kitchen and household
source_excerpt: It constitutes the tarnish that forms over time on silverware and other silver objects.

extra.why_interesting: The egg clue is the foothold: anyone who has smelled an overcooked egg knows that rotten-egg stink. Connecting that smell to the black on grandma's spoons is the 'of course' moment.
extra.verification_notes: Silver tarnish is silver sulfide, and H2S causes the rotten-egg smell, so sulfur is correct (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_sulfide).

explanation: Eggs are rich in sulfur-containing proteins and give off hydrogen sulfide, which reacts with silver to form black silver sulfide. A bowl lined with aluminium foil, hot water and baking soda reverses the reaction.

question: Overcooked green vegetables turn a drab olive colour because acids in the pot knock which metal out of the centre of the chlorophyll molecule?
topic: Chemistry of the kitchen and household
source_excerpt: pheophytin is a chlorophyll molecule lacking a central Mg2+ ion. It can be produced from chlorophyll by treatment with a weak acid

extra.why_interesting: Players know iron sits in blood; few know chlorophyll has its own metal. The foothold is that a metal must be there to be knocked out, and magnesium is the plant-world answer.
extra.verification_notes: Acid treatment removes the central Mg2+ from chlorophyll to give pheophytin (olive-brown when cooked); the cooking colour detail comes from background knowledge, not the fetched page.

explanation: Just as iron sits at the heart of the red pigment in blood, magnesium sits at the heart of chlorophyll. Lose it and the pigment turns brownish, which is why a pinch of baking soda keeps beans bright green, at the cost of making them mushy.

question: Cream of tartar, which bakers add to stabilise whipped egg whites, is a crystalline by-product of making which drink?
topic: Chemistry of the kitchen and household
source_excerpt: its crude precipitate form tartar or wine stone are byproducts of winemaking found deposited on top of must barrels which can be purified.

extra.why_interesting: Nobody expects a baking-cupboard powder to come from a cellar. The word 'tartar' is a foothold for players who know tartaric acid from wine, giving them a fair route in.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms cream of tartar (potassium bitartrate) is a crystalline byproduct of winemaking and is used to stabilise egg whites.

explanation: It is potassium bitartrate, which forms as crusty crystals on the inside of wine barrels and tanks as the wine ages. Winemakers scrape it off and it is purified into the fine white powder in your cupboard.

question: Cola is sometimes poured on rusty bolts to loosen them. Which acid, which gives cola its sharp tang, is also the active ingredient in many rust removers?
topic: Chemistry of the kitchen and household
source_excerpt: Food-grade phosphoric acid (additive E338) is used to acidify foods and beverages such as various colas and jams, providing a tangy or sour taste.

extra.why_interesting: The rusty-bolt trick sounds like an urban legend. The reveal is that it is real, and the acid responsible is a named ingredient on the label that players have read a hundred times.
extra.verification_notes: Phosphoric acid gives cola its tang and is used in rust treatment/removers, per Wikipedia https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phosphoric_acid

explanation: Phosphoric acid reacts with iron oxide to form a dark compound that lifts off or stops further rusting. The amount in a drink is tiny, so the bolt trick is slow, but the chemistry is exactly the same as in a hardware-store rust remover.

question: Mixing household bleach with which other common cleaning chemical releases toxic chloramine gas?
topic: Chemistry of the kitchen and household
source_excerpt: In dilute aqueous solution, chloramine is prepared by the reaction of ammonia with sodium hypochlorite: NH3 + NaOCl → NH2Cl + NaOH

extra.why_interesting: Players assume stronger cleaning means mixing more products; the twist is that two of the most ordinary bottles under the sink become a chemical weapon when combined, and knowing which pair matters in real life.
extra.verification_notes: Bleach (sodium hypochlorite) reacts with ammonia to form chloramine, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chloramine; no contradicting or newer information found.

explanation: Bleach is sodium hypochlorite, and when it meets ammonia it forms chloramine vapours that attack the lungs. It is why cleaning labels warn you never to combine products in one bucket.

question: Baking soda only makes a cake rise if the batter also contains something like buttermilk or lemon juice. Baking powder needs no such help. What type of ingredient is pre-mixed into baking powder that plain baking soda lacks?
topic: Chemistry of the kitchen and household
source_excerpt: Baking powder is a dry chemical leavening agent, a mixture of a carbonate or bicarbonate and a weak acid.

extra.why_interesting: Most home cooks treat baking soda and baking powder as interchangeable white powders and have been burned by a flat, soapy-tasting cake. The answer reframes the difference as a chemistry fact: one of them is only half a reaction, and the other comes with its partner built in.
extra.verification_notes: Baking powder is a mixture of bicarbonate and a weak acid, while baking soda is only sodium bicarbonate, so the answer 'an acid' is correct (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baking_powder).

explanation: Baking soda is a base and only releases carbon dioxide when it meets an acid, so baking powder bundles a dry acid such as cream of tartar in with it. Add water and the fizz starts on its own, which is why you can't simply swap one for the other.

question: Roman launderers, called fullers, placed pots on street corners and asked passers-by to urinate in them, then let the contents stand for days before pouring it over woollen togas. Why did this actually help clean the clothes?
correct_answer: Stale urine releases ammonia, which dissolves grease
alternative_answers: It is alkaline and strips grease
It works like soap or bleach
Urea breaks down into ammonia, a cleaning agent
headline_answer: Stale urine releases ammonia, which dissolves grease
source_excerpt: a mixture of alkaline chemicals (sometimes including ammonia derived from urine)

extra.verification_notes: Ammonia from (aged) urine as a grease-dissolving alkali in Roman fulling is the standard explanation; I found no contradicting source, though the page only supports the ammonia point and not the aging detail (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fullonica).

explanation: As urine stands, bacteria break down the urea in it into ammonia. Ammonia is alkaline, so it loosens grease, sweat and dirt from wool fibres and brightens white cloth, much like a modern detergent. The fullers trampled the garments in vats of this aged urine mixed with water, then rinsed and dried them. The trade was so profitable that Emperor Vespasian taxed the collection of urine, and when his son Titus complained, Vespasian reportedly held a coin to his nose and said money does not smell, the origin of the Latin saying pecunia non olet.

question: Condemned by an Athenian jury in 399 BC, the philosopher Socrates was executed by drinking a cup of which poison?
source_excerpt: The jurors favoured the death penalty by making him drink a cup of hemlock (a poisonous liquid).

extra.why_interesting: A well-known classic with a clear one-word answer; the surprise is that a philosopher was condemned to death by his own city for asking too many questions.
extra.verification_notes: Socrates was sentenced in 399 BC and executed by drinking hemlock, per Wikipedia.

explanation: Socrates was found guilty of corrupting the youth and impiety, and calmly drank the hemlock while his students watched, as Plato describes in the Phaedo.

question: True or false: Julius Caesar was the first emperor of Rome.
source_excerpt: Julius Caesar was made Rome's first dictator perpetuo...and then assassinated on the Ides of March (15 March).

extra.why_interesting: Caesar is the most famous Roman of all and his name became the word for emperor, so most people assume he was one; he was killed before the empire even existed.
extra.verification_notes: Augustus, not Julius Caesar, was the first Roman emperor (27 BC–AD 14); Caesar was dictator perpetuo and was assassinated before the empire began, so 'False' is correct (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus).

explanation: Caesar ruled as dictator of the Republic and was assassinated in 44 BC; the first emperor was his adopted heir Octavian, who took the title Augustus in 27 BC.

question: According to legend, the founders of Rome, Romulus and Remus, were nursed as babies by which wild animal?
source_excerpt: the twins were suckled by a she-wolf in a cave now known as the Lupercal.

extra.why_interesting: A story most players have half-heard; the pleasure is the instant recall of the bronze wolf image that still symbolises Rome today.
extra.verification_notes: The she-wolf nursing the twins is the standard legend; the woodpecker only brought food, so the answer is not ambiguous (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romulus_and_Remus).

explanation: The she-wolf suckling the twins became the enduring emblem of Rome, and a bronze statue of her is still displayed on the Capitoline Hill.

question: The Rosetta Stone carries the same decree in three different scripts, but in only two languages. Which language appears on it twice?
source_excerpt: It bears three inscriptions: the top register in Ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs, the second in the Egyptian Demotic script, and the third in Ancient Greek.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone remembers 'three scripts' and assumes three languages; realising two of the scripts are the same language is a small aha that explains why the stone was decipherable.
extra.verification_notes: Stone has hieroglyphic and Demotic (both Egyptian) plus Greek, so Egyptian appears twice, as claimed.

explanation: The stone is written in hieroglyphic script, in Demotic script, and in Greek, and the first two are both forms of the Egyptian language, which is what let Champollion crack the hieroglyphs using the Greek.

question: The Greek inventor Archimedes, famous for shouting 'Eureka', spent his life in the city of Syracuse. In which modern country is Syracuse?
source_excerpt: Archimedes is estimated to have been born c. 287 BC in the seaport city of Syracuse, Sicily.

extra.why_interesting: Archimedes is the archetypal ancient Greek, so players reach for Greece; the answer reminds them the Greek world stretched far beyond modern Greece.
extra.verification_notes: Archimedes was born in and associated with Syracuse, Sicily, which is in modern Italy (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archimedes).

explanation: Syracuse was a powerful Greek colony on Sicily, and Archimedes was killed there when the Romans captured the city in 212 BC, far from mainland Greece.

question: The Colosseum in Rome did not get its name from its own size. What enormous object standing next to it gave the arena its nickname?
source_excerpt: The name Colosseum is believed to be derived from a colossal statue of Nero on the model of the Colossus of Rhodes.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the name describes the building's own size; it actually borrowed the name from a neighbour that has since vanished.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia states the name Colosseum is believed to derive from the colossal statue of Nero that stood beside the amphitheatre.

explanation: The building was officially the Flavian Amphitheatre, but a roughly 30-metre bronze Colossus of Nero stood beside it, and the nickname stuck long after the statue was gone.

question: In which year did Howard Carter open the nearly intact tomb of Tutankhamun in Egypt's Valley of the Kings?
source_excerpt: Tutankhamun's tomb was discovered in 1922 by excavators led by Howard Carter and his patron, George Herbert, 5th Earl of Carnarvon.

extra.why_interesting: The gold mask feels timeless, so players struggle to place the discovery; anchoring it in the roaring twenties, between the two world wars, is the satisfying click.
extra.verification_notes: Carter discovered Tutankhamun's tomb in 1922, and 1922 is the only plausible option; the burial chamber was opened in 1923 but that is not among the choices (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tutankhamun).

explanation: Carter found the sealed steps in November 1922, and the discovery set off a worldwide Egypt craze that shaped 1920s fashion and design.

question: More than a thousand years before Cleopatra, which woman ruled Egypt as a full pharaoh and had herself portrayed in statues wearing the ceremonial false beard of a king?
source_excerpt: Hatshepsut eventually assumed the position of pharaoh alongside him by Year 7 of his reign, c. 1472 BC.

extra.why_interesting: Players know Cleopatra as the female ruler of Egypt; learning that an earlier woman took the full male regalia of a pharaoh, beard included, is the surprise, and Cleopatra is the tempting wrong answer.
extra.verification_notes: Hatshepsut ruled c. 1479–1458 BC as full pharaoh and was depicted with a false beard; Sobekneferu and Twosret are also pre-Cleopatra female pharaohs, but the beard detail points to Hatshepsut (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hatshepsut).

explanation: Hatshepsut reigned for around two decades in the 15th century BC, and her successors later tried to erase her name and smash her beard-wearing statues.

question: For the first thirteen ancient Olympic Games, there was only one event, lasting under half a minute. What kind of contest was it?
source_excerpt: The only event recorded at the first thirteen games was the stade, a straight-line sprint of just over 192 metres (630 ft).

extra.why_interesting: Players picture the ancient Games as a full festival of wrestling, discus and chariots from day one; the fact that the whole competition was a single short sprint for over fifty years overturns that, and the stem's 'one length of the stadium' gives a fair reasoning foothold.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the stade, a ~192 m straight sprint, was the only event at the first thirteen ancient Olympics.

explanation: The stadion was a sprint of roughly 190 metres, one length of the stadium at Olympia, and it stood alone from 776 BC until a longer race was added in 724 BC. Wrestling, boxing and chariot racing all came later.

question: Many medieval castle walls flare outward at the bottom into a sloping base called a talus. Apart from making the wall thicker, what practical advantage did this slope give defenders standing on top of the wall?
correct_answer: Dropped stones bounce outward into attackers
alternative_answers: Rocks ricochet off the slope at attackers
Keeps battering rams and siege towers away from the wall
Harder to place ladders against the wall
Harder to tunnel under or mine the wall
Makes the base too thick to breach
headline_answer: Dropped stones bounce outward into attackers
source_excerpt: Defenders are also able to drop rocks over the walls, which will shatter on the talus, spraying a hail of shrapnel into any attackers massed at the base of the wall.

extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms dropped rocks striking the talus spray shrapnel outward into attackers; 'bounce' vs 'shatter' is a minor wording difference.

explanation: On a vertical wall, a rock dropped from the battlements falls straight down and lands at the foot of the wall. On a talus, the falling rock strikes the slope and ricochets outward, scattering into the attackers crowded below. The slope also kept battering rams and siege towers from getting flush against the wall, made ladders harder to place, and resisted undermining by sappers because the base was far thicker than the top.

question: Richard the Lionheart died in 1199 while besieging a small castle in France. What kind of weapon fired the shot that killed him?
source_excerpt: A crossbow bolt struck Richard in the shoulder on 26 March 1199

extra.why_interesting: The great warrior king of the Crusades did not fall in a glorious battle but to a single bolt during a minor siege over a petty dispute.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Richard I was struck by a crossbow bolt at Châlus-Chabrol in March 1199 and died of the gangrenous wound on 6 April.

explanation: A bolt struck him in the shoulder and the wound turned gangrenous, so the most famous crusader king died over a squabble with a minor vassal at Châlus.

question: On Friday the 13th of October 1307, King Philip IV of France had the members of which order of warrior monks arrested across his kingdom?
source_excerpt: At dawn on Friday, 13 October 1307, King Philip IV had de Molay and scores of other French Templars simultaneously arrested.

extra.why_interesting: The date itself is the hook: a famous 'unlucky' Friday the 13th that really did end a mighty order of knights.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Philip IV had the Templars arrested at dawn on Friday 13 October 1307.

explanation: The deeply indebted king accused the Templars of heresy, seized their wealth, and five years later the pope dissolved the order entirely.

question: True or false: Neuschwanstein, the famous fairytale castle in Bavaria, was built in the Middle Ages.
source_excerpt: The foundation stone for the palace was laid on 5 September 1869

extra.why_interesting: The world's most 'medieval-looking' castle is a 19th-century fantasy, built roughly at the same time as railways and the telephone.
extra.verification_notes: Neuschwanstein was begun in 1869 under Ludwig II, so it is not medieval; the answer False is correct (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuschwanstein_Castle).

explanation: Construction began in 1869 for King Ludwig II of Bavaria, so the castle is younger than the first railways and was still unfinished when Ludwig died in 1886.

question: Roughly how much did a complete suit of knight's plate armour weigh?
source_excerpt: A complete suit of plate armour made from well-tempered steel would weigh around 15–25 kg (33–55 lb).

extra.why_interesting: The popular image is of knights hoisted onto horses by cranes; in reality a full harness weighed about as much as a modern soldier's kit.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia gives 15–25 kg for a full plate suit, which best matches the 20–30 kg option and rules out the other three.

explanation: A full field harness came in at around 20 to 25 kilograms, comparable to a modern infantry soldier's load, and a trained knight could run, mount a horse and climb in it.

question: In which year did the Alhambra palace fortress in Granada, the last Muslim stronghold in Spain, surrender to Ferdinand and Isabella?
source_excerpt: the last vestige of Al-Andalus

extra.why_interesting: Players rarely connect the fall of the Alhambra with the year everyone knows for Columbus; it was the same monarchs in the same year.
extra.verification_notes: Granada's surrender was agreed in Nov 1491 and completed on 2 Jan 1492, so 1492 is the conventional answer and the other options are clearly wrong (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitulation_of_Granada).

explanation: Granada fell in January 1492, and a few months later the same Ferdinand and Isabella signed off on Columbus's voyage across the Atlantic.

question: Krak des Chevaliers, the Crusader castle that Lawrence of Arabia called perhaps the finest in the world, stands in which modern country?
source_excerpt: perhaps the best preserved and most wholly admirable castle in the world

extra.why_interesting: Players picture Crusader castles in the Holy Land and guess Israel or Jordan; the greatest of them all is in Syria, a country rarely associated with medieval tourism.
extra.verification_notes: Krak des Chevaliers is in Homs Governorate, Syria, and the Lawrence quote is accurately paraphrased; no changes in location or borders are recorded (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krak_des_Chevaliers).

explanation: The castle sits on a hill near Homs in western Syria, and its concentric walls still stand largely intact after eight centuries.

question: Malbork Castle in Poland, the largest castle in the world by land area, was built as the headquarters of which order of crusading knights?
source_excerpt: It was constructed by the Teutonic Order, a German Catholic religious order of crusaders. It is the largest castle in the world measured by land area

extra.why_interesting: Players expect the biggest castle to be in Britain or France; it is a vast brick fortress in Poland built not by a king but by crusading German monks.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Malbork Castle was built by the Teutonic Order, which made it its headquarters in 1309, and that it is the largest castle by land area.

explanation: The Teutonic Order moved its grand master to Malbork in 1309 and turned it into a brick fortress covering about 21 hectares, now a UNESCO World Heritage site.

question: Which king of France died in 1559 after a splintered lance went through his eye during a celebratory jousting tournament?
source_excerpt: Henry, wearing the colours of his mistress Diane de Poitiers, was wounded in the eye by a fragment of the splintered lance of Gabriel Montgomery

extra.why_interesting: Jousting seems like a staged pageant, yet it killed a reigning king and effectively ended the sport in France.
extra.verification_notes: Henry II of France died in 1559 after Montgomery's splintered lance wounded his eye at a tournament celebrating the Peace of Cateau-Cambrésis and his daughter's marriage (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_II_of_France).

explanation: Henry was jousting to celebrate a peace treaty and his daughter's wedding when a splinter from his opponent's lance pierced his visor, and he died ten days later.

question: Which fortified city in southern France, protected by two rings of walls and more than fifty towers, gave its name to a hugely popular tile-laying board game?
source_excerpt: The fortified city consists essentially of a concentric design of two outer walls with 52 towers and barbicans to prevent attack by siege engines.

extra.why_interesting: Many players have placed the game's little tiles without realising the name belongs to a real double-walled city they could visit.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Carcassonne's double walls with 52 towers and that the tile-laying board game is named after it.

explanation: The medieval citadel of Carcassonne is a UNESCO World Heritage site, and the board game named after it has sold millions of copies since 2000.

question: In 1969 Prince Charles was formally invested as Prince of Wales at which castle, built by Edward I to subdue the Welsh?
source_excerpt: Prince Charles was invested at Caernarvon Castle in north Wales on July 1, 1969.

extra.why_interesting: A castle built by an English king to crush Wales became the stage for a modern royal ceremony watched by millions on television.
extra.verification_notes: Charles was invested as Prince of Wales at Caernarfon Castle on 1 July 1969; the castle was built by Edward I after his conquest of Wales, and nothing newer changes this.

explanation: Edward I's son, the first English Prince of Wales, was born at Caernarfon in 1284, which is why the castle was chosen for the televised ceremony nearly seven centuries later.

question: Bran Castle in Transylvania draws hundreds of thousands of visitors a year because of its link to which fictional character?
source_excerpt: the claimed connection between the castle and the Dracula legend is tourism-driven

extra.why_interesting: A real medieval fortress owes its fame almost entirely to a fictional vampire its historical occupants never met.
extra.verification_notes: Bran Castle is marketed as 'Dracula's Castle', tied to Stoker's fictional Count Dracula; the link is tourism-driven, but the question asks about a fictional character, so Dracula is correct.

explanation: Bram Stoker never visited Romania, and there is no evidence Vlad the Impaler ever lived at Bran, but the castle is sold to tourists as Dracula's home all the same.

question: After the Ottomans drove them from Rhodes, the Knights Hospitaller were given which Mediterranean island by Emperor Charles V in 1530?
source_excerpt: In exchange for providing Malta, Gozo, and the North African port of Tripoli in perpetual fiefdom, Charles V would receive an annual fee of a single Maltese falcon

extra.why_interesting: An entire island nation's identity comes from a homeless crusading order that got a new base for the price of one bird a year.
extra.verification_notes: Charles V granted Malta (with Gozo and Tripoli) to the Hospitallers in 1530 after their expulsion from Rhodes; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knights_Hospitaller.

explanation: The order's rent was a single falcon delivered to the emperor each year, and the knights ruled Malta for more than two and a half centuries until Napoleon arrived.

question: Which crusading English king, celebrated as a national hero, spent only about six months of his ten-year reign actually inside England?
source_excerpt: Following his accession to the crown of England, he spent very little time, perhaps as little as six months, in England.

extra.why_interesting: Players picture him as the archetypal English king of the Robin Hood era, yet he barely set foot in the country he ruled and reportedly spoke little or no English.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia says Richard I spent 'perhaps as little as six months' in England during his 1189–1199 reign, which matches the question.

explanation: Richard I spent his reign crusading, held for ransom in Germany, and fighting in France, treating England mostly as a source of money for his wars.

question: During the Second World War, Allied engineers studied bombers that returned from missions and mapped where they had been hit by enemy fire. A statistician then advised them to add armour to the parts of the aircraft that showed NO bullet holes. Why?
correct_answer: Planes hit there never came back
alternative_answers: Hits in those areas were fatal
The planes hit there were shot down
Damage in the marked areas was survivable, so the unmarked areas must be the deadly ones
The shot-down planes were missing from the data
headline_answer: Planes hit there never came back
source_excerpt: the damaged portions of returning planes show locations where they can sustain damage and still return home; those hit in other places presumedly do not survive.

extra.verification_notes: Wald's survivorship-bias reasoning matches the answer: planes hit in the unmarked areas didn't return (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Wald).

explanation: The engineers only saw the survivors. Bullet holes on the returning planes marked places where a bomber could take damage and still fly home, such as the wings and fuselage. The areas that were clean, like the engines and cockpit, were clean because any plane hit there was shot down and never made it back to be studied. The statistician Abraham Wald recognised this flaw, now known as survivorship bias, and recommended armouring the apparently untouched sections instead.

question: In June 1940, Hitler had an old railway carriage hauled out of a museum so that France could sign its surrender inside it. What had been signed in that very carriage in November 1918?
correct_answer: The Armistice ending World War One
alternative_answers: Germany's surrender in World War One
source_excerpt: On 21 June 1940, the car was removed from its museum building and placed on the exact spot it had been in 1918.

extra.why_interesting: The player assumes the carriage was just a convenient venue; the twist is that Hitler chose it deliberately to reverse the humiliation of 1918.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the carriage was removed from its museum building in June 1940 and was the site of the 11 November 1918 armistice signing (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compiègne_Wagon).

explanation: The carriage stood in the forest of Compiègne, where Germany had accepted defeat in 1918, and Hitler staged the 1940 ceremony there to turn that humiliation around.

question: Japanese lieutenant Hiroo Onoda kept fighting in the jungle of Lubang Island in the Philippines because no one had officially told him the war was over. In which decade did he finally surrender?
source_excerpt: Onoda surrendered on March 10, 1974, after nearly 29 years of hiding.

extra.why_interesting: Players know some soldiers held out after 1945 but assume a few years at most; the correct decade is almost three decades after the war ended.
extra.verification_notes: Onoda surrendered on March 10, 1974, which is in the 1970s; the 'never officially told' premise is a simplification (leaflets were dropped), but the answer is unambiguous (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiroo_Onoda).

explanation: Onoda laid down his rifle in March 1974, nearly 29 years after Japan surrendered, and only after his former commanding officer flew out to relieve him of duty in person.

question: Switzerland was one of the last countries in Europe to give women the vote in national elections. In which year did Swiss men finally approve it in a referendum?
source_excerpt: Women in Switzerland gained the right to vote in federal elections after a referendum in February 1971

extra.why_interesting: Players assume a wealthy Western democracy enfranchised women after WWI or WWII; the true year is in the era of the Moon landings.
extra.verification_notes: Swiss men approved federal women's suffrage in the February 1971 referendum (the 1959 attempt failed); no later event changes this, per Wikipedia.

explanation: Men voted it through in February 1971, more than half a century after Germany and Britain, and one canton held out on local votes until a court forced it in 1990.

question: True or false: Japan and Russia have still never signed a formal peace treaty ending the Second World War.
source_excerpt: a permanent peace treaty between Japan and Russia has not been concluded

extra.why_interesting: Players assume every WWII belligerent made formal peace decades ago; the claim sounds like a trick, but it is true.
extra.verification_notes: No Japan-Russia peace treaty has been signed; talks were suspended by Russia in 2022 and relations have deteriorated through 2026 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuril_Islands_dispute).

explanation: A 1956 declaration restored diplomatic relations, but the dispute over the Kuril Islands seized by the Soviet Union in 1945 has blocked a full peace treaty ever since.

question: In November 1939, the Soviet Union attacked a small neighbour and was expelled from the League of Nations for it. Which country was invaded?
source_excerpt: The USSR invaded Finland on 30 November 1939... the League of Nations deemed the attack illegal and expelled the Soviet Union

extra.why_interesting: Players remember Poland as the 1939 victim and forget the Soviets attacked a second neighbour that winter; the expulsion detail is the surprise.
extra.verification_notes: The USSR invaded Finland on 30 Nov 1939 and was expelled from the League of Nations for it (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winter_War).

explanation: The Winter War saw the badly outnumbered Finns hold off the Red Army for over three months, and the League's expulsion of the Soviets was one of its last meaningful acts.

question: Which of these Nordic countries stayed neutral and was never invaded or at war during the Second World War?
source_excerpt: Sweden maintained official neutrality throughout WWII and was never invaded or formally at war.

extra.why_interesting: Four Nordic neighbours look identical on the surface; the player must know which one managed to stay out of the fighting entirely.
extra.verification_notes: Sweden remained officially neutral and was never invaded or formally at war in WWII, while Norway and Denmark were invaded and Finland fought the USSR and Germany (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweden_during_World_War_II).

explanation: Germany occupied Denmark and Norway in April 1940, and Finland fought two wars against the Soviet Union, while Sweden kept out by trading with both sides.

question: The 1936 Summer Olympics were turned into a showcase for the Nazi regime, famously undermined when American sprinter Jesse Owens won four gold medals. Which city hosted those Games?
source_excerpt: The 1936 Summer Olympics...were an international multi-sport event held from 1 to 16 August 1936 in Berlin, Germany.

extra.why_interesting: Easy entry question with a clear foothold: the propaganda angle points straight to Nazi Germany's capital.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the 1936 Summer Olympics were held in Berlin and that Jesse Owens won four golds (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1936_Summer_Olympics).

explanation: The Games were awarded to Germany before Hitler took power, and he used them to present a polished face to the world while Owens stole the show on the track.

question: The deadliest pandemic of the 20th century broke out in 1918. By what name is it commonly known, borrowed from a neutral country whose newspapers were simply free to report on it?
source_excerpt: Spain was a neutral country unconcerned with appearances of combat readiness

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the name marks where the disease began; in fact it only marks the one country honest enough to print the news.
extra.verification_notes: Spanish flu is named for neutral Spain's free press reporting on the 1918 pandemic; the 'deadliest of the 20th century' phrasing is conventional, with a minor HIV/AIDS caveat only. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_flu

explanation: Spain was neutral in the First World War, so its press covered the outbreak openly while censors in the fighting nations kept quiet, and the unfair name stuck.

question: Wojtek was officially enlisted as a private in the Polish army, had his own paybook, and hauled crates of artillery shells at Monte Cassino in 1944. What kind of animal was he?
source_excerpt: Wojtek was officially drafted into the Polish Army as a private and listed among the soldiers of the 22nd Artillery Supply Company

extra.why_interesting: An enlisted soldier with a rank and a service record turns out to be a bear; the clues about size and strength let a thoughtful player reason their way there.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Wojtek was a Syrian brown bear enlisted as a private with a paybook who carried shell crates at Monte Cassino; no newer development contradicts this.

explanation: Wojtek was a Syrian brown bear adopted as a cub by Polish soldiers in Iran, and he spent his retirement at Edinburgh Zoo, where former comrades came to visit him.

question: In 1943 British intelligence let a dead body carrying fake invasion plans wash up on the Spanish coast, convincing Hitler the Allies would land in Greece. Which Mediterranean island was the real target?
source_excerpt: the discovered Anglo-Saxon order confirms the assumption that the planned attacks will be directed mainly against Sardinia and the Peloponnesus.

extra.why_interesting: The scheme sounds too absurd to have worked; players can reason from the 1943 Mediterranean timeline to the real target.
extra.verification_notes: Operation Mincemeat deceived Germany about the Allied target; the real invasion target was Sicily (Operation Husky), per Wikipedia.

explanation: Operation Mincemeat worked so well that German forces were shifted toward Greece and Sardinia, and the Allied landing on Sicily that July met weaker resistance than expected.

question: The Molotov cocktail got its name as a joke at the expense of the Soviet foreign minister. Soldiers of which country coined it while fighting the Red Army in the winter of 1939 to 1940?
source_excerpt: The name 'Molotov cocktail' was coined by the Finns during the Winter War in 1939.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the weapon was named by or for the Soviets; it was in fact a joke at Molotov's expense by the small country he was attacking.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the Finns coined the name during the Winter War as mockery of Molotov.

explanation: Molotov claimed Soviet planes were dropping food to starving Finns, so the Finns called the cluster bombs Molotov bread baskets and offered a drink to go with them.

question: Alan Turing's team at Bletchley Park built on an earlier breakthrough: mathematicians from which country first cracked the German Enigma cipher, back in 1932?
source_excerpt: In December 1932, Marian Rejewski made what historian David Kahn describes as one of the greatest advances in cryptologic history, by applying pure mathematics

extra.why_interesting: Nearly everyone credits Alan Turing and Bletchley Park with cracking Enigma. The player starts from Britain and has to remember that a different country's mathematicians had already broken it years before the war even started.
extra.verification_notes: Polish mathematician Marian Rejewski first broke military Enigma in December 1932, as stated on Wikipedia's Cipher Bureau (Poland) page.

explanation: Marian Rejewski and his colleagues at the Polish Cipher Bureau reconstructed the Enigma machine with pure mathematics, and in July 1939 Poland handed its methods and replica machines to Britain and France, giving Bletchley Park a seven-year head start.

question: Germany made its very last reparations payment for the First World War in which year?
source_excerpt: The final payment was made on 3 October 2010, settling German loan debts in regard to reparations.

extra.why_interesting: The player assumes reparations were a 1920s and 1930s story that Hitler simply cancelled. The answer lands in the age of smartphones, decades after the last trench was filled in.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the final payment settling WWI reparation-related loan debts was made on 3 October 2010; no newer event supersedes it.

explanation: Hitler stopped payments in 1933, but West Germany took the debt back on in 1953 and agreed that interest on some bonds would wait until the country was reunified. That final bill of around seventy million euros was paid on 3 October 2010, exactly twenty years after reunification.

question: Many dinosaurs lived in lush, wet, forested landscapes, yet palaeontologists find most of their fossils in dry deserts and barren badlands rather than in today's forests. Why?
correct_answer: Erosion exposes bare rock; nothing covers it
alternative_answers: No soil or plants hide the rock
The rock layers are exposed at the surface
Wind and rain erode the ground and uncover bones
Forests bury fossils under soil and vegetation
You can only see fossils where rock is bare
The land was different then; today's deserts expose old rock
headline_answer: Erosion exposes bare rock; nothing covers it
source_excerpt: Deserts, rivers, mountains and badlands are excellent locations for fossil discovery, due to high levels of erosion that occurs in these locales.

extra.verification_notes: Standard explanation: erosion in arid badlands exposes fossil-bearing strata with little vegetation cover, while forests hide the rock (Live Science).

explanation: Fossils form inside layers of sedimentary rock, and you can only find them where that rock reaches the surface. In a forest, the rock lies hidden under soil, roots and dense vegetation, and plant cover slows erosion, so bones stay buried. In deserts and badlands there is almost no soil or vegetation, so wind and occasional heavy rain strip the land down to the rock itself and keep cutting new surfaces. That constant erosion brings bones that were buried for tens of millions of years out into the open, where a fossil hunter can spot them. The dinosaurs did not live in deserts; the deserts are simply where their graves are easiest to see.

question: Prehistoric insects are sometimes found perfectly preserved inside which golden fossilised substance, which began as sticky tree resin?
source_excerpt: because it originates as a soft, sticky tree resin, amber sometimes contains animal and plant material as inclusions.

extra.why_interesting: Players picture fossils as bones in rock; the idea that a whole insect can survive intact inside what was once tree sap is a pleasing reminder that fossils come in other forms.
extra.verification_notes: Amber is fossilized tree resin that often contains preserved insect inclusions, per Wikipedia.

explanation: Resin oozing from ancient trees trapped insects, spiders and even small lizards, then hardened and fossilised over millions of years into amber.

question: Roughly 180 kilometres wide and mostly buried, the crater left by the asteroid blamed for killing the dinosaurs lies on the edge of the Yucatán Peninsula in which country?
source_excerpt: The impact structure is situated in Mexico, specifically beneath the Yucatán Peninsula.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone knows an asteroid killed the dinosaurs, but far fewer can say where it actually hit; the answer turns a vague cosmic story into a place on a map.
extra.verification_notes: Chicxulub crater is ~180 km wide, buried, and located at the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico per Wikipedia.

explanation: The Chicxulub crater straddles the coast near the town of the same name, half under land and half under the Gulf of Mexico, and was only identified as an impact site around 1990.

question: Megalodon, the prehistoric giant whose name means 'big tooth', was what kind of animal?
source_excerpt: Megalodon is an extinct species of giant mackerel shark that lived approximately 23 to 3.58 million years ago

extra.why_interesting: Megalodon is often lumped in with dinosaurs in popular imagination; players enjoy confirming it was a shark that lived long after the dinosaurs were gone.
extra.verification_notes: Megalodon (Otodus megalodon) is an extinct giant mackerel shark whose name means 'big tooth'; reclassification only changed its genus and family, not that it is a shark (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megalodon).

explanation: Megalodon was a shark perhaps 15 to 20 metres long, and it swam the oceans millions of years after the last dinosaurs had died, going extinct only around 3.6 million years ago.

question: Scientists insist the dinosaurs never fully died out. Which group of animals alive today is formally classified as true dinosaurs?
source_excerpt: Birds are the only extant members of Dinosauria, and are a type of paravian theropods.

extra.why_interesting: Players start from 'dinosaurs are extinct'; the answer reframes the pigeon on the windowsill as a living theropod.
extra.verification_notes: Birds are the only extant members of Dinosauria, as stated on Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bird).

explanation: Birds descend from small feathered theropods related to Velociraptor, so in modern classification a sparrow is as much a dinosaur as Tyrannosaurus rex.

question: Non-bird dinosaurs first appeared in the Triassic period and vanished 66 million years ago. Roughly how long did their reign on Earth last?
source_excerpt: Dinosaurs may have appeared as early as the Anisian epoch of the Triassic, approximately 243 million years ago

extra.why_interesting: Players know dinosaurs were around 'a very long time' but rarely subtract the two dates; realising the reign lasted well over 150 million years, versus a few hundred thousand for our species, is humbling.
extra.verification_notes: Dinosaurs appeared ~230-233 Ma and ended 66 Ma, giving ~165-170 million years; the other options are far off (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinosaur).

explanation: Dinosaurs appeared around 230 million years ago, so they dominated the land for roughly 165 million years, which is more than 500 times longer than Homo sapiens has existed.

question: Which of these famous prehistoric animals was not a dinosaur?
source_excerpt: Dimetrodon is often mistaken for a dinosaur or portrayed as a contemporary of dinosaurs in popular culture, but it became extinct by the middle Permian, some 40 million years before

extra.why_interesting: Dimetrodon appears in nearly every toy dinosaur set, so players assume it belongs; discovering it is closer to us than to T. rex is a genuine surprise.
extra.verification_notes: Dimetrodon is a Permian synapsid, not a dinosaur; the other three are dinosaurs (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimetrodon).

explanation: Dimetrodon lived in the Permian, tens of millions of years before any dinosaur, and belongs to the synapsid line that eventually led to mammals, which makes it a closer relative of ours than of Stegosaurus.

question: Tyrannosaurus rex is famous for its tiny arms. How many clawed fingers did each of those hands carry?
source_excerpt: The forelimbs had only two clawed fingers, along with an additional splint-like small third metacarpal representing the remnant of a third digit.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone jokes about T. rex's tiny arms, but almost nobody has counted the fingers; the answer is a satisfying detail hiding in plain sight on every museum skeleton.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms T. rex forelimbs had two clawed fingers plus a vestigial splint-like third metacarpal; no newer findings contradict this.

explanation: Each stubby arm ended in just two clawed fingers, down from three in earlier tyrannosaur relatives, though the arms were still strong enough to lift well over a hundred kilograms.

question: Which famous long-necked sauropod name, scrapped in 1903 as merely a species of Apatosaurus, was officially revived as a valid genus by a 2015 study?
source_excerpt: the two genera may be regarded as synonymous

extra.why_interesting: Many adults were told as children that Brontosaurus 'never existed'; learning the name was officially rehabilitated in 2015 is a delightful reversal.
extra.verification_notes: Riggs synonymized Brontosaurus with Apatosaurus in 1903, and Tschopp et al. 2015 revalidated it as a genus; some researchers still dispute this, but the question's claim holds.

explanation: After more than a century as a supposed mistake, a detailed 2015 analysis of sauropod skeletons found Brontosaurus different enough from Apatosaurus to earn its old name back.

question: Which deep-sea fish, believed extinct for 66 million years, turned up alive in a trawler's catch off South Africa in 1938?
source_excerpt: off the east coast of South Africa, off the Chalumna River

extra.why_interesting: Players assume extinction is final; a fish turning up in a fishing net 66 million years after its supposed demise is one of the great Lazarus stories of science.
extra.verification_notes: The coelacanth was found alive in December 1938 off the Chalumna River, South Africa, after being thought extinct since the Late Cretaceous (~66 million years ago); the trawler detail rests on my recollection of the Nerine, not on the fetched page.

explanation: Museum curator Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer spotted the strange blue fish in a trawler's haul, and it proved to be a coelacanth, a lineage known until then only from fossils older than the dinosaurs' extinction.

question: Which spiral-shelled marine fossils, common in museum gift shops, were named after the coiled ram's horns worn by an Egyptian god?
source_excerpt: Pliny the Elder called fossils of these animals ammonis cornua ('horns of Ammon')

extra.why_interesting: Ammonites sit in every museum shop, yet almost no one connects the familiar spiral to an Egyptian deity; the ram's-horn image makes the link click instantly once heard.
extra.verification_notes: Ammonites are named from Pliny's 'ammonis cornua' (horns of Ammon), the Egyptian god depicted with ram's horns, per Wikipedia.

explanation: The Roman writer Pliny the Elder called these coiled shells the horns of Ammon, after the ram-headed god Amun, and the name ammonite stuck for the extinct relatives of squid and octopus.

question: Oviraptor was named 'egg thief' in 1924 because its skeleton was found lying on a nest of eggs. What did later discoveries show it had actually been doing there?
source_excerpt: findings of numerous oviraptorosaurs in nesting poses have demonstrated that this specimen was actually brooding the nest and not stealing nor feeding on the eggs.

extra.why_interesting: The animal was condemned by its own name for seventy years; learning the supposed thief was actually a devoted parent is a reversal with real emotional pull.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the holotype was found over a nest and later nesting oviraptorosaur finds show it was brooding the nest, not stealing eggs.

explanation: Fossils found in the 1990s revealed oviraptorid embryos inside identical eggs and adults crouched over nests with arms spread, proving the so-called thief was a parent keeping its own clutch warm, bird-style.

question: Fossils of dinosaurs have been dug up on how many of Earth's seven continents?
source_excerpt: Over the last few decades, paleontologists have found fossils there from four dinosaurs including the fearsome meat-eater Cryolophosaurus.

extra.why_interesting: Players picture dinosaurs in deserts of Mongolia or the American West and assume the frozen south is out of the question. The answer that no continent is dinosaur-free, Antarctica included, overturns that, and a player can reason their way there via Pangaea.
extra.verification_notes: Dinosaur fossils are known from every continent including Antarctica (Cryolophosaurus, Antarctic sauropod), so 'all seven' holds; see https://eartharchives.org/articles/dinosaurs-of-the-south-pole/index.html

explanation: Even Antarctica has produced dinosaurs such as the crested Cryolophosaurus, because the continents were still joined as Pangaea when dinosaurs appeared and Antarctica was then forested and mild.

question: Every match of the 2010 World Cup in South Africa was played to the constant drone of which long plastic horn?
source_excerpt: The intensity of the sound caught the attention of the global football community during the 2009 FIFA Confederations Cup in anticipation of South Africa hosting the 2010 FIFA World Cup.

extra.why_interesting: Players remember the sound before the football; the horn became more famous than most of the matches.
extra.verification_notes: The vuvuzela is the long plastic horn that defined the 2010 South Africa World Cup soundscape; no newer events can change this historical fact.
