explanation: Thousands of them blown at once produced a single bee-swarm buzz, and broadcasters scrambled to filter it out of their sound feeds.

question: The Games officially branded 'Tokyo 2020' were the first Olympics ever postponed rather than cancelled. In which year did they actually take place?
source_excerpt: the Tokyo Games were postponed until 2021 on March 24, 2020 as a result of the global COVID-19 pandemic, the only such postponement in the history of the Olympic Games

extra.why_interesting: The name says 2020, which is exactly the trap; the twist is that earlier Games were cancelled outright but never postponed.
extra.verification_notes: Tokyo 2020 was postponed and held 23 July–8 August 2021, the only Olympic postponement in history, per Wikipedia.

explanation: They kept the 2020 name and logo but ran in the summer of 2021, mostly in empty stadiums, because of the pandemic.

question: Which Caribbean island nation sent a bobsleigh team to the 1988 Calgary Winter Olympics, a story that later became the film Cool Runnings?
source_excerpt: Their participation went on to inspire the 1993 film Cool Runnings.

extra.why_interesting: A tropical island with no snow competing in a sled race is the kind of mismatch that sticks in memory for decades.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Jamaica's bobsleigh team competed at Calgary 1988 and inspired Cool Runnings; no newer event invalidates this.

explanation: The four-man sled crashed on its third run, and the crew walked it across the finish line to a standing ovation.

question: The 2022 World Cup was the first ever played in November and December instead of the traditional June and July. Why?
source_excerpt: To avoid the extremes of Qatar's hot climate in summers, the event was held in November and December.

extra.why_interesting: The whole football calendar was torn up for the first time in history, and the reason is a simple matter of weather.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the 2022 World Cup was the first held in Nov-Dec, moved to avoid Qatar's extreme summer heat.

explanation: Qatar's daytime temperatures in June and July can pass 40 degrees Celsius, so the tournament was shifted to the mildest part of the year.

question: Months before the 1966 World Cup in England, the trophy was stolen from an exhibition in London. A week later it turned up wrapped in newspaper under a garden hedge. Who found it?
source_excerpt: Pickles began to sniff at a parcel that was lying under the hedge of Corbett's house. It was wrapped in an old newspaper, tied with string.

extra.why_interesting: Players expect a detective or a police tip-off; the hero of the national crisis turns out to be a mongrel on a walk.
extra.verification_notes: Pickles the dog found the stolen Jules Rimet Trophy wrapped in newspaper a week after its 20 March 1966 theft; sources differ only on hedge versus car wheel, which does not affect the answer.

explanation: Pickles sniffed it out while on a walk in south London, became a national celebrity and was even invited to the winners' banquet.

question: One medal event of the Paris 2024 Olympics was held at Teahupo'o in French Polynesia, nearly 16,000 km from Paris. Which sport?
source_excerpt: Teahupoʻo reef pass, Tahiti, French Polynesia

extra.why_interesting: An Olympic event on the other side of the planet from the host city sounds absurd until you remember France owns a legendary wave in the Pacific.
extra.verification_notes: Surfing was the only sport held at Teahupo'o in Tahiti at Paris 2024; the distance is roughly right (15,000–15,700 km) and nothing newer contradicts it.

explanation: Teahupo'o is home to one of the heaviest reef waves on Earth, and as French territory it let Paris stage Olympic surfing on a real Pacific swell.

question: True or false: solo synchronized swimming, with one swimmer performing entirely alone, was once an official Olympic medal event.
source_excerpt: A Women's Solo event was removed from the Olympic program after the 1992 Olympic Games.

extra.why_interesting: The phrase sounds like a joke about being synchronized with nobody, so players bet it is false; it really existed for three Olympics.
extra.verification_notes: Women's solo was an Olympic medal event in 1984, 1988 and 1992 and was removed afterwards, so 'was once' is correct (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synchronized_swimming_at_the_Summer_Olympics).

explanation: It was contested at three Games from 1984 to 1992, with the swimmer synchronized to the music rather than to a partner, before being replaced by the team event.

question: The torch relay carrying the Olympic flame from Olympia in Greece to the host city feels ancient, but it was invented for which Games?
source_excerpt: The Olympic flame and the Olympic torch relay was first introduced to the Summer Olympics at the 1936 Summer Olympics in Berlin by Carl Diem.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the relay is an ancient Greek tradition or a founding ritual of 1896; it was in fact invented for the Nazi-era Berlin spectacle.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the Olympia-to-host-city torch relay was first introduced at Berlin 1936 by Carl Diem; no later event changes this.

explanation: Berlin 1936 staged the first relay, with thousands of runners carrying the flame across Europe, and every Games since has copied the idea.

question: The record for most goals by one player at a single World Cup, thirteen, has stood since 1958. Which Frenchman set it?
source_excerpt: Just Fontaine set a record in Sweden that will likely never be broken: 13 goals in a single World Cup.

extra.why_interesting: Fans assume a modern superstar holds the scoring record; it belongs to a Frenchman from 1958 whose team did not even reach the final.
extra.verification_notes: Fontaine's 13 goals at the 1958 World Cup still stands; the 2026 Golden Boot winner Mbappé scored only 10 (https://www.skysports.com/football/news/13564837/world-cup-2026-golden-boot-race-kylian-mbappe-beats-lionel-messi-to-become-top-goalscorer).

explanation: Fontaine scored in every match in Sweden, including four in the third-place game, and no one has come within four goals of him since.

question: Only one national team has played at every single men's football World Cup since the first in 1930. Which country?
source_excerpt: Brazil is also the only national team to have played in all FIFA World Cup editions without any absence or need for play-offs.

extra.why_interesting: Players expect several football giants to share this record. In fact Germany, Italy, Argentina and others have all missed at least one tournament, leaving a single survivor.
extra.verification_notes: Brazil remains the only nation to have played in every World Cup, including 2026, per Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil_at_the_FIFA_World_Cup).

explanation: Every other heavyweight has missed at least one edition, whether through failing to qualify or by staying home in the early years. Brazil's unbroken run stretches all the way back to the first tournament in Uruguay.

question: Uruguay's national football shirt carries four stars, yet the country has won only two World Cups. What do the other two stars commemorate?
source_excerpt: This is why Uruguay is allowed to display four stars on its football crest, despite having won the FIFA World Cup twice (in 1930 and 1950).

extra.why_interesting: Stars on a shirt are supposed to mean World Cups, so four stars against two titles looks like a mistake. The resolution is that before the World Cup existed, another tournament served as the world championship.
extra.verification_notes: Uruguay's four stars represent the 1924 and 1928 Olympic titles plus the 1930 and 1950 World Cups, so the answer holds and nothing newer overturns it.

explanation: Uruguay won football gold at the 1924 and 1928 Olympics, the de facto world championships before the World Cup was created. FIFA recognises those titles, so Uruguay wears all four.

question: For almost forty years, from 1912 to 1948, Olympic medals were awarded in five categories including architecture, literature and music. What was this overall competition for?
source_excerpt: architecture, literature, music, painting, and sculpture

extra.why_interesting: The player assumes every Olympic medal has rewarded physical performance. The five named fields are footholds that point away from sport entirely, and the payoff is that Olympic medallists include poets and composers.
extra.verification_notes: Olympic art competitions ran 1912–1948 with five categories (architecture, literature, music, painting, sculpture) per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_Olympic_Games; nothing newer supersedes this.

explanation: Pierre de Coubertin wanted the Games to unite muscle and mind, so painters, sculptors, writers, composers and architects competed with sport-themed works. The contests were dropped after 1948 because the artists were professionals in an amateur-only era.

question: The 2014 World Cup was staged in Brazil. Which team won it, becoming the first European side ever to lift the trophy at a tournament held in the Americas?
source_excerpt: Germany's victory marked the first World Cup win by a European team in the Americas.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the Americas were always home turf for South American champions; the 2014 result broke an eighty-four-year streak that most fans never consciously noticed, and the host year is a strong foothold to the answer.
extra.verification_notes: Germany beat Argentina 1-0 in the 2014 final in Brazil, the first European World Cup win in the Americas; a later 2026 tournament in the Americas doesn't change that Germany was first (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_FIFA_World_Cup_final).

explanation: Germany beat Argentina one-nil in the final at the Maracanã. In every earlier World Cup hosted in the Americas, a South American team had taken the title.

question: The 1992 Winter Olympics were held in Albertville, France. In which year were the very next Winter Olympics held?
source_excerpt: The 1994 Winter Olympics were held from 12 to 27 February 1994 in Lillehammer, Norway.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone knows the Olympics come every four years, so the reflex answer is 1996. The real gap was only two years, the one time in history the cycle was deliberately broken.
extra.verification_notes: The 1994 Winter Olympics in Lillehammer immediately followed Albertville 1992, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_Winter_Olympics.

explanation: Lillehammer in Norway hosted just two years later. The IOC decided the Winter and Summer Games should no longer share a year, so it shortened one cycle to split them apart for good.
